vaquita.hook: The smallest porpoise, confined to one corner of the Gulf of California — a 2025 survey saw about 7–10 different animals.
vaquita.imageAlt: A vaquita porpoise surfacing, showing its dark back and triangular dorsal fin
vaquita.what: The vaquita is a small porpoise found only in the upper Gulf of California, Mexico. IUCN lists it as Critically Endangered. The 2025 joint visual survey (IUCN Cetacean Specialist Group / SEMARNAT) used expert elicitation: a 67 percent probability that observers saw 7–10 different individuals, compared with 6–8 in 2024 and 8–12 in 2023. Those are minimums inside the study area, not a finished census. A full abundance estimate is promised for 2026. The founder figure “fewer than about 10” matches the recent sighting counts; it is not a proven total.
vaquita.range: A few thousand square kilometres of shallow water in the northern Gulf of California. It has no other home.
vaquita.story: Gillnets set for totoaba — a fish whose swim bladder is valuable in illegal trade — drown vaquitas as bycatch. A zero-tolerance zone and net bans have not stopped the fishing. The decline is recent and steep: from hundreds in the late twentieth century to a handful now. Calves were still photographed in 2025.
vaquita.when: Critically Endangered now, because of people. Extinction is a near-term risk.
vaquita.humanRole: Illegal gillnets, not climate or a shrinking Ice Age range, are the cause.
vaquita.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Phocoena sinus, CR); IUCN-CSG / SEMARNAT Vaquita Research Campaign 2025 survey report.

amur-tiger.hook: The northernmost tiger — a few hundred animals in the Russian Far East and northeast China.
amur-tiger.imageAlt: An Amur tiger walking through a snowy forest
amur-tiger.what: The Amur, or Siberian, tiger is the northern subspecies of Panthera tigris. IUCN assesses the tiger species as Endangered (2022). Amur animals live in temperate mixed forest, not jungle, and take deer, wild boar, and occasionally larger prey.
amur-tiger.range: Southwest Primorye and Khabarovsk in Russia, plus a recovering presence in northeast China. The subspecies once ranged into the Korean Peninsula and more of Manchuria.
amur-tiger.story: Hunting and forest loss erased tigers from most of Northeast Asia. Russian and Chinese protection, plus prey recovery, raised Amur numbers from a few dozen in the mid-twentieth century to the high hundreds in 2010s–2020s surveys (published figures vary; roughly 500–750 is a commonly cited recent range). Roads, poaching, and thin prey still limit them.
amur-tiger.when: Endangered as a tiger; the Amur population is a small, guarded remnant.
amur-tiger.humanRole: We hunted the tiger to the edge here; protection, not empty wilderness, explains the partial rebound.
amur-tiger.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Panthera tigris, Endangered, 2022); Russian and Chinese range-wide counts (estimates).

Tama Zoological Park, Tokyo Zoological Park Society: Tiger (Amur tiger)

sumatran-orangutan.hook: A great ape of northern Sumatra, listed Critically Endangered as oil palm replaces forest.
sumatran-orangutan.imageAlt: A Sumatran orangutan sitting in the fork of a tree
sumatran-orangutan.what: The Sumatran orangutan is one of three living orangutan species, confined to northern Sumatra. IUCN lists it as Critically Endangered. The 2017 assessment estimated about 13,800 animals and a continuing decline. It is mostly arboreal and eats fruit.
sumatran-orangutan.range: Aceh and North Sumatra, especially the Leuser ecosystem. It no longer occurs in southern Sumatra. Bornean and Tapanuli orangutans are separate species.
sumatran-orangutan.story: Logging, oil-palm plantations, roads, killing, and the pet trade have cut and isolated the forest. Orangutans breed slowly; a forest that looks green on a map can already be too small. The last 20,000 years on Sumatra included much more continuous lowland forest than remains.
sumatran-orangutan.when: Critically Endangered, declining, because of people.
sumatran-orangutan.humanRole: Forest conversion — especially oil palm — plus hunting is the cause.
sumatran-orangutan.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Pongo abelii, Critically Endangered, 2017 estimate ~13,800).

black-rhino.hook: Horn poaching cut the species to a few thousand; a partial recovery still leaves it Critically Endangered.
black-rhino.imageAlt: A black rhinoceros standing in open grassland
black-rhino.what: The black rhinoceros is a browsing African rhino with a prehensile upper lip. IUCN lists it as Critically Endangered. The western subspecies is extinct (see that entry). Remaining animals are in eastern and southern Africa, many in fenced conservancies.
black-rhino.range: Once much of sub-Saharan Africa. Now scattered strongholds, especially Namibia, Kenya, South Africa, and Zimbabwe.
black-rhino.story: Horn demand collapsed numbers from on the order of 100,000 around 1960 to about 2,400 in the mid-1990s. Intensive protection then produced a rebound: the International Rhino Foundation’s 2025 compilation, citing IUCN African Rhino Specialist Group figures, put the total near 6,788 at the end of 2024. That is an estimate, and it is still a fragment of the mid-century population.
black-rhino.when: Critically Endangered now. The western subspecies is already gone.
black-rhino.humanRole: The horn trade is the main driver; habitat loss adds pressure.
black-rhino.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Diceros bicornis, CR); IRF State of the Rhino 2025 (end-2024 estimate).

sources.label: University of Michigan Museum of Zoology, Animal Diversity Web: Diceros bicornis (black rhinoceros)
Save the Rhino International: Black rhinos

african-forest-elephant.hook: Listed Critically Endangered in 2021 after an estimated 80 percent decline over three generations.
african-forest-elephant.imageAlt: An African forest elephant standing among trees
african-forest-elephant.what: The African forest elephant is a distinct species of the Congo Basin and West African forests, smaller than the savanna elephant, with straighter tusks. IUCN listed it Critically Endangered in 2021, the first time the two African elephants were assessed separately.
african-forest-elephant.range: Central African rainforest, especially Gabon, Congo, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, plus isolated West African forests.
african-forest-elephant.story: Ivory poaching along logging roads, and the conversion of forest, drove the crash. The 2021 assessment estimated a decline of more than 80 percent over three generations. A 2024 African Elephant Specialist Group status report, and later DNA surveys, found additional animals; the Critically Endangered listing stands.
african-forest-elephant.when: Critically Endangered now, primarily because of people.
african-forest-elephant.humanRole: Ivory and the opening of forest interiors are the main causes.
african-forest-elephant.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Loxodonta cyclotis, CR, 2021); AfESG forest-elephant status work, 2024.

mountain-gorilla.hook: The only great ape whose counted numbers have risen — still Endangered, and only in two highland forests.
mountain-gorilla.imageAlt: A mountain gorilla sitting in dense green vegetation
mountain-gorilla.what: The mountain gorilla is a subspecies of the eastern gorilla, living at high elevation in the Virunga volcanoes and in Bwindi. IUCN downlisted it from Critically Endangered to Endangered in 2018. The eastern gorilla species as a whole remains Critically Endangered.
mountain-gorilla.range: Two adjacent highland blocks: the Virunga Massif (DRC, Rwanda, Uganda) and Bwindi–Sarambwe (Uganda/DRC). There is no other wild population.
mountain-gorilla.story: Snares, farmland at the forest edge, and disease remain threats. Coordinated patrols and veterinary care raised the counted total to 1,063 when the 2015–16 Virunga survey was combined with the 2018 Bwindi–Sarambwe census. That is the best recent published global figure; it is still a tiny range.
mountain-gorilla.when: Endangered now. Numbers are up because of protection, not because pressure ended.
mountain-gorilla.humanRole: We squeezed the forest and set snares; intensive guarding is why the count rose.
mountain-gorilla.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Gorilla beringei beringei, EN, 2018); IGCP/WWF census release, 1,063.

amur-leopard.hook: One of the rarest big cats — on the order of 100–130 mature animals in one transboundary forest.
amur-leopard.imageAlt: An Amur leopard facing forward, showing a thick spotted winter coat
amur-leopard.what: The Amur, or Far Eastern, leopard is the northernmost leopard subspecies, adapted to snowy temperate forest. IUCN lists it as Critically Endangered. Camera-trap studies in the 2020s have produced estimates around 100–130 mature individuals (WWF and IUCN citations around 130 in 2023) — more than “several dozen adults,” which was a mid-2000s picture. Every total is still an estimate.
amur-leopard.range: A small area of southwest Primorye in Russia and adjacent Jilin and Heilongjiang in China. The historical range included more of Northeast Asia and the Korean Peninsula.
amur-leopard.story: Prey hunting, poaching for skins, forest fire, and roads reduced the leopard to one landscape. A national park on the Russian side and camera-trap monitoring on both sides of the border are why a population still exists. It has not recolonised its old map.
amur-leopard.when: Critically Endangered now, because of people.
amur-leopard.humanRole: Hunting and habitat loss left a single remnant; protection, not isolation from humans, keeps it alive.
amur-leopard.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Panthera pardus orientalis, CR); WWF/IUCN camera-trap estimates, early 2020s.

hawksbill-turtle.hook: A coral-reef turtle hunted for tortoiseshell and still listed Critically Endangered.
hawksbill-turtle.imageAlt: A hawksbill sea turtle swimming, showing its pointed beak and patterned shell
hawksbill-turtle.what: The hawksbill is a tropical sea turtle with a bird-like beak and overlapping shell scutes. Those scutes are the source of traditional tortoiseshell. IUCN lists the species as Critically Endangered. The last full assessment (2008) estimated a decline of more than 80 percent over three generations; the listing has not been relaxed.
hawksbill-turtle.range: Coral reefs and tropical coasts of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans. Nesting is on sandy beaches; feeding is on sponges on reefs.
hawksbill-turtle.story: People have taken hawksbills for shell, eggs, and meat for centuries. Modern fisheries add bycatch, and damaged reefs remove food. CITES has banned international tortoiseshell trade since 1977 for this species, but illegal trade and local harvest continue.
hawksbill-turtle.when: Critically Endangered now, primarily because of people.
hawksbill-turtle.humanRole: The shell trade, egg harvest, and fishing gear are the main causes.
hawksbill-turtle.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Eretmochelys imbricata, CR, 2008 assessment still current); CITES Appendix I. Russian name: бисса.

northern-white-rhinoceros.hook: Two living females remain. The subspecies is functionally extinct in the wild; it is not a recovering herd.
northern-white-rhinoceros.imageAlt: Angalifu, a northern white rhinoceros, grazing in a grassy enclosure
northern-white-rhinoceros.what: The northern white rhinoceros is a subspecies of the white rhino (Ceratotherium simum cottoni), a wide-mouthed grazer of African grassland. Only two animals are alive: Najin and her daughter Fatu, both females, kept under guard at Ol Pejeta Conservancy in Kenya. The last male, Sudan, died in March 2018. IUCN treats the white rhino species as Near Threatened because the southern subspecies still numbers in the tens of thousands; this northern form is Critically Endangered and gone as a wild breeding population.
northern-white-rhinoceros.range: Historically South Sudan, Uganda, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Chad. The last wild animals were in Garamba National Park. There is no wild population now.
northern-white-rhinoceros.story: Horn poaching and war emptied the range. The two survivors cannot produce a calf without assisted reproduction. The BioRescue consortium has made northern-white embryos and transferred some into southern-white surrogates; as of 2025–2026 no long-term pregnancy has been reported. That is a laboratory hope, not a wild recovery.
northern-white-rhinoceros.when: Functionally extinct in the wild. Two captive females remain.
northern-white-rhinoceros.humanRole: The horn trade and conflict finished the wild animals. Captive care keeps two females alive; it has not restored a population.
northern-white-rhinoceros.sourcesNote: Save the Rhino / IRF population notes; Ol Pejeta and Leibniz-IZW BioRescue updates; IUCN Red List (Ceratotherium simum).

javan-rhinoceros.hook: The rarest living rhino — one park on Java, and a 2025 count near 50 after poaching.
javan-rhinoceros.imageAlt: Historical photograph of a Javan rhinoceros standing in a London Zoo enclosure
javan-rhinoceros.what: The Javan rhinoceros is a one-horned Asian rhino, smaller than the greater one-horned rhino of India and Nepal. IUCN lists it as Critically Endangered. Every remaining animal lives in Ujung Kulon National Park, West Java. The International Rhino Foundation’s 2025 compilation put the total near 50, down from about 76, after an organised poaching ring took up to 26 animals between 2019 and 2023. Older “70–80” figures predate that loss.
javan-rhinoceros.range: Ujung Kulon only. The species once ranged through much of Southeast Asia, including Vietnam, where the last mainland animal was poached in 2010.
javan-rhinoceros.story: A single park means a single flood, disease, or volcano can finish the species. Camera traps and dung DNA are how Indonesia counts them. There is no second wild population to fall back on.
javan-rhinoceros.when: Critically Endangered now. One landscape, tens of animals.
javan-rhinoceros.humanRole: Historical hunting shrank the map; recent poaching inside the last park cut the count again.
javan-rhinoceros.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Rhinoceros sondaicus, CR); IRF State of the Rhino 2025; Save the Rhino population page.

sumatran-rhinoceros.hook: The smallest, hairiest living rhino — IRF estimates 34–47 in the wild, not a comfortable “under 80.”
sumatran-rhinoceros.imageAlt: A Sumatran rhinoceros looking out from dense rainforest leaves
sumatran-rhinoceros.what: The Sumatran rhinoceros is the only living two-horned Asian rhino and the hairiest. IUCN lists it as Critically Endangered. The International Rhino Foundation’s 2025 figures, unchanged from 2022, estimate 34–47 animals in the wild, plus a handful in the Sumatran Rhino Sanctuary at Way Kambas. Isolated forest pockets often hold animals that never meet a mate.
sumatran-rhinoceros.range: Fragments of Sumatra and, at vanishing densities, possibly still a few on Borneo. The historical range ran from the Himalayan foothills through mainland Southeast Asia.
sumatran-rhinoceros.story: Poaching emptied most forests; roads and oil palm then isolated the rest. A semi-wild breeding programme at Way Kambas has produced calves. That is an insurance herd, not a restored wild population.
sumatran-rhinoceros.when: Critically Endangered now, in the low tens.
sumatran-rhinoceros.humanRole: Horns and forest conversion. Remaining animals persist because of fences, patrols, and managed breeding.
sumatran-rhinoceros.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Dicerorhinus sumatrensis, CR); IRF State of the Rhino 2025 (34–47).

saola.hook: The “Asian unicorn” — a forest bovid science met in 1992, last photographed in 2013, with no honest head-count.
saola.imageAlt: A saola standing in dense Annamite forest, looking back toward the camera
saola.what: The saola is a dark forest bovid with long, almost parallel horns, the only species in its genus. It is not an antelope and not a unicorn. IUCN lists it as Critically Endangered. There is no census. The IUCN SSC Saola Working Group has said realistic guesses fall below 100, and some specialists think the true number is far lower or already zero. Exact numbers are unknown.
saola.range: Wet evergreen forest in the Annamite Mountains of Vietnam and Laos. It has never been confirmed in Cambodia.
saola.story: Western science named the species from hunter trophies in 1992–93. A few animals died quickly in captivity; a 2013 camera-trap frame is the last widely accepted wild photograph. The main killer is indiscriminate snaring for other trade species, not a market that wants saola itself. Search teams in 2024–25 have not published a new confirmed detection.
saola.when: Critically Endangered now. Last confirmed wild photograph: 2013.
saola.humanRole: Industrial snaring of Annamite forests — bycatch of a species people barely knew existed.
saola.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Pseudoryx nghetinhensis, CR); IUCN SSC Saola Working Group position statement, 2021.

yangtze-giant-softshell-turtle.hook: The largest living freshwater turtle — a few known individuals, and no confirmed breeding female since 2023.
yangtze-giant-softshell-turtle.imageAlt: A Yangtze giant softshell turtle with a mottled head and leathery shell, photographed at Dong Mo Lake
yangtze-giant-softshell-turtle.what: Rafetus swinhoei is a huge softshell turtle of large rivers and lakes in China and northern Vietnam. IUCN lists it as Critically Endangered. After the Suzhou Zoo female died in 2019 and the last confirmed wild female died at Dong Mo Lake in April 2023, only a few animals are known: a captive male in Suzhou and at least one wild turtle at Xuan Khanh, sex unconfirmed. Others may still hide; eDNA surveys are looking. That is not a breeding population.
yangtze-giant-softshell-turtle.range: Historically the Yangtze and Red River systems. Today, a zoo in Jiangsu and a handful of lakes near Hanoi — if those animals are still alive.
yangtze-giant-softshell-turtle.story: Hunting and dams emptied the rivers. Captive breeding failed. Without a known fertile female, the species is functionally extinct even if a male or two remain. Claims of more animals need photographs or DNA, not hope.
yangtze-giant-softshell-turtle.when: Critically Endangered now. Last confirmed female: 2023.
yangtze-giant-softshell-turtle.humanRole: Overharvest and river engineering left a species with almost no individuals to count.
yangtze-giant-softshell-turtle.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Rafetus swinhoei, CR); Asian Turtle Program / Mongabay reports on the 2023 Dong Mo death.

kakapo.hook: A flightless New Zealand parrot. The official tally in 2026 is 325 named birds, and the species is still critically endangered.
kakapo.imageAlt: Sirocco the kākāpō, a moss-green flightless parrot, facing the camera among flax leaves
kakapo.what: The kākāpō is the world’s heaviest parrot, nocturnal and flightless. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Critically Endangered. New Zealand’s Department of Conservation added 90 independent 2026 chicks on 1 September 2026, taking the official tally from 235 to 325, a recovery-era high, from 51 birds when the modern programme began in 1995. Every bird is named and tagged. The population is still tiny and island-bound.
kakapo.range: Predator-free islands (Whenua Hou, Pukenui, Te Kākahu) plus a fenced mainland trial at Maungatautari. Once widespread on both main islands.
kakapo.story: Māori hunting and, later, cats, stoats, and rats erased the mainland bird. Intensive management, with nest minding, supplementary food, and genetic pairing, produced the 2026 jump. Islands are filling up.
kakapo.when: Critically Endangered now. The birds are counted and managed, and one predator incursion could still undo the work.
kakapo.humanRole: Introduced mammals caused the crash; people now keep every remaining bird alive by hand.
kakapo.sourcesNote: New Zealand Department of Conservation media release, 1 September 2026 (325 birds); International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List (Strigops habroptilus, Critically Endangered).

axolotl.hook: A gilled salamander of Mexico City’s canals — common in tanks, nearly gone from Xochimilco.
axolotl.imageAlt: A wild-type dark axolotl facing the camera underwater among stones
axolotl.what: The axolotl is a paedomorphic salamander: it keeps larval gills and lives in water as an adult. IUCN lists it as Critically Endangered. Wild animals survive only in remnant canals of Xochimilco (and unstable scraps of former lakes). Density estimates fell from about 6,000 per km² in 1998 to about 35 per km² by 2014. A UNAM census in 2024–25 caught none in nets; environmental DNA still found the species. IUCN’s assessment band is tens to about a thousand mature wild animals — not a precise count. Captive pet and lab stocks are huge and genetically mixed; they are not the wild population.
axolotl.range: High-altitude canals and chinampa waterways on the south edge of Mexico City. The old lake system has been drained.
axolotl.story: Drainage, sewage, pesticides, and introduced carp and tilapia wrecked the canals. Chinampa-refuge projects try to fence out the fish. A pet shop full of pink axolotls is not a recovered species.
axolotl.when: Critically Endangered in the wild now.
axolotl.humanRole: We drained and polluted the only home, then bred the animal as a curiosity.
axolotl.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Ambystoma mexicanum, CR); Zambrano / UNAM density series; UNAM–CI Xochimilco census 2024–25.

chinese-giant-salamander.hook: The largest amphibian — farmed by the tens of thousands, wild lineages collapsing, and not one species.
chinese-giant-salamander.imageAlt: A Chinese giant salamander underwater in a zoo tank, showing a broad flat head and wrinkled skin
chinese-giant-salamander.what: Chinese giant salamanders are the world’s largest living amphibians. They were long treated as one species, Andrias davidianus. Genetics now show a complex: named forms include A. davidianus, A. sligoi (the South China giant salamander), A. jiangxiensis, and A. cheni, plus further unnamed clades (Yan et al. 2018; Turvey and later reviews). IUCN still assesses A. davidianus as Critically Endangered; A. sligoi has a separate CR listing. Wild numbers are not a single honest total.
chinese-giant-salamander.range: Hill streams of central, southern, and eastern China, historically in the Yellow, Yangtze, and Pearl basins. Farm stock has been moved far outside native drainages.
chinese-giant-salamander.story: A luxury-food farming boom from the 2000s vacuumed wild animals for brood stock. A 2013–16 survey of 97 likely sites found salamanders at only four, and those may have been farm escapees (Turvey et al. 2018). Mass releases of farmed A. davidianus are homogenising wild gene pools. “Millions on farms” is not wild recovery.
chinese-giant-salamander.when: Critically Endangered in the wild now. Taxonomy is still being split.
chinese-giant-salamander.humanRole: Food markets and restocking with the wrong lineage — overharvest plus genetic pollution.
chinese-giant-salamander.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Andrias davidianus, CR; A. sligoi, CR); Turvey et al. 2018; Yan et al. 2018; ZSL Chinese giant salamander action plan.

addax.hook: A spiral-horned Sahara antelope — tens left in the last wild desert, plus a reintroduction in Chad.
addax.imageAlt: An addax with long corkscrew horns and a dark forehead patch standing on dry ground
addax.what: The addax is the only species in its genus, a white desert antelope that can live without free water. IUCN listed it as Critically Endangered in 2016, when fewer than 100 wild animals were thought to remain, mostly in Niger’s Tin Toumma. Noé camel patrols in 2023 still found only small groups there. Sahara Conservation’s October 2024 survey of the reintroduced Chad population estimated about 100 after a harsh dry-season die-off. Captive herds are large; they are not the Sahara remnant.
addax.range: Once the Sahara from Mauritania to Sudan. Wild remnants: eastern Niger. Reintroduced animals: Ouadi Rimé–Ouadi Achim, Chad, and fenced sites in North Africa.
addax.story: Motorised hunting, then oil roads and insecurity, emptied the desert. A 2019 reserve-boundary change in Niger left core addax habitat outside protection. Reintroduction is real and still fragile.
addax.when: Critically Endangered now. Wild plus reintroduced animals remain in the low hundreds at most.
addax.humanRole: Hunting with vehicles, then extraction infrastructure in the last range.
addax.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Addax nasomaculatus, CR, 2016); Sahara Conservation 2024 annual report; Noé Tin Toumma monitoring.

sources.label: University of Michigan Museum of Zoology, Animal Diversity Web: Addax nasomaculatus (addax)

cao-vit-gibbon.hook: One of the rarest apes — 74 animals in 11 families, not the older count of 120.
cao-vit-gibbon.imageAlt: Preserved holotype of the Cao Vit gibbon in a museum jar, labelled Hylobates nasutus
cao-vit-gibbon.what: The Cao Vit, or eastern black crested gibbon, is a singing ape of limestone forest. IUCN lists it as Critically Endangered. A 2021 survey using vocal fingerprinting and drone thermal counts estimated 74 individuals in 11 family groups on the Vietnam–China border (Wearn et al. 2024, Scientific Reports). Earlier triangulation had double-counted groups and published about 120. Living field photographs are scarce; the card image is the Paris holotype.
cao-vit-gibbon.range: A single karst forest patch under 5,000 hectares, split between Trung Khanh (Vietnam) and Bangliang (China).
cao-vit-gibbon.story: Hunting and charcoal-cutting reduced the ape to this scrap. Infants are still being born. The forest is too small for a safe future without restored corridors. The Hainan gibbon (Nomascus hainanus) is a different species.
cao-vit-gibbon.when: Critically Endangered now. One forest, tens of animals.
cao-vit-gibbon.humanRole: Hunting and clearance left one remnant; patrols, not empty wilderness, keep it.
cao-vit-gibbon.sourcesNote: Wearn et al. 2024, Scientific Reports (74 in 11 groups); IUCN Red List (Nomascus nasutus, CR).

devils-hole-pupfish.hook: A fish of one Nevada spring — dozens to low hundreds on a single limestone shelf.
devils-hole-pupfish.imageAlt: Iridescent blue Devils Hole pupfish swimming over the cavern’s rocky shelf
devils-hole-pupfish.what: The Devils Hole pupfish lives only in Devils Hole, a water-filled limestone cavern in a detached unit of Death Valley National Park, inside Ash Meadows National Wildlife Refuge, Nevada. IUCN lists it as Critically Endangered. Almost the entire wild life cycle happens on a shelf of about 215 square feet. Spring counts have swung from a 25-year high of 191 in 2024 to 38 after earthquake seiches in spring 2025, then 77 in spring 2026. A captive refuge population is held at the Ash Meadows Fish Conservation Facility.
devils-hole-pupfish.range: One hole in the Mojave Desert. Nowhere else.
devils-hole-pupfish.story: Groundwater pumping once threatened the water level (Cappaert v. United States, 1976). Earthquakes, thin algae, and a gene pool of dozens keep the count violent. In 2025 managers released captive-bred fish into the hole for the first time. “Dozens in one spring” is the honest long-run picture, even when a good year hits the low hundreds.
devils-hole-pupfish.when: Critically Endangered now. One spring, a fluctuating handful.
devils-hole-pupfish.humanRole: Aquifer pumping was the historic threat; the species now survives as a managed relic.
devils-hole-pupfish.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Cyprinodon diabolis, CR); NPS spring 2025 count; USFWS 2026 update (77).

chinese-pangolin.hook: An Asian scaly anteater listed Critically Endangered after the scale-and-meat trade.
chinese-pangolin.imageAlt: A Chinese pangolin walking, showing overlapping keratin scales
chinese-pangolin.what: The Chinese pangolin is a nocturnal, scale-covered mammal that eats ants and termites. IUCN listed it as Critically Endangered in 2019. There is no reliable range-wide head-count; assessments infer collapse from trade seizures and empty forests. It is one of four Asian pangolins. African pangolins (giant and white-bellied Endangered; Temminck’s and black-bellied Vulnerable) are a separate trade stream, not this card.
chinese-pangolin.range: Historically from northern India and Nepal through southern China to Taiwan and northern Southeast Asia. Now a scatter of remnants.
chinese-pangolin.story: Scales enter traditional-medicine markets; meat is a luxury food. CITES moved all pangolins to Appendix I in 2017. Poaching and smuggling continue. Habitat loss adds pressure. Do not invent a global number.
chinese-pangolin.when: Critically Endangered now, because of people.
chinese-pangolin.humanRole: Commercial hunting for scales and meat is the main driver.
chinese-pangolin.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Manis pentadactyla, CR, 2019); IUCN SSC Pangolin Specialist Group; CITES Appendix I.

sunda-pangolin.hook: Southeast Asia’s most heavily trafficked pangolin — Critically Endangered, no honest census.
sunda-pangolin.imageAlt: A Sunda pangolin climbing, showing a long prehensile scaled tail
sunda-pangolin.what: The Sunda, or Malayan, pangolin is the most widespread Asian pangolin, more arboreal than the Chinese species. IUCN listed it as Critically Endangered in 2019, inferring an 80 percent decline over about three generations from trade and local reports. No robust population total exists. Hundreds of thousands of animals have appeared in seizure records since the 1970s; that is a minimum of what was taken, not a living count.
sunda-pangolin.range: Mainland Southeast Asia, Sumatra, Java, Borneo, and some smaller islands. Already rare or gone in large parts of that map.
sunda-pangolin.story: As Chinese pangolins thinned, traffickers shifted to Sunda animals. Forest loss for oil palm and pulp adds a second cut. Night surveys still find them in a few protected forests; that is not abundance.
sunda-pangolin.humanRole: International scale trade plus local meat hunting.
sunda-pangolin.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Manis javanica, CR, 2019); Challender et al. trade syntheses; CITES Appendix I.

philippine-pangolin.hook: A Palawan endemic listed Critically Endangered — trade plus a tiny island range.
philippine-pangolin.imageAlt: 2015 Philippine postage stamp illustrating a Philippine pangolin on a branch
philippine-pangolin.what: The Philippine, or Palawan, pangolin is a separate species confined to the Palawan faunal region. IUCN listed it as Critically Endangered in 2019 (up from Endangered). Density estimates are local and old; there is no island-wide census. Free photographs of living animals are scarce on public archives, which is why this card uses a 2015 Philippine stamp.
philippine-pangolin.range: Palawan and associated islands (including Culion and Dumaran). Nowhere else.
philippine-pangolin.story: Local hunting for meat and scales, plus export into the same East Asian trade that emptied Chinese and Sunda forests, hit a species that never had a continent to hide in. Habitat conversion on Palawan adds pressure.
philippine-pangolin.humanRole: Hunting and trade on a small island range.
philippine-pangolin.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Manis culionensis, CR, 2019); Lagrada et al. assessments; CITES Appendix I.

indian-pangolin.hook: South Asia’s pangolin — Endangered, not Critically Endangered, and still in the same trade.
indian-pangolin.imageAlt: An Indian pangolin walking on stone paving, showing large overlapping scales
indian-pangolin.what: The Indian pangolin is a large, mostly terrestrial pangolin of the Indian subcontinent. IUCN listed it as Endangered in 2019, a step below the three other Asian species (all CR). There is still no credible range-wide count. As Chinese and Sunda stocks fell, seizures of Indian pangolins rose — a classic sequential-exploitation pattern.
indian-pangolin.range: India, Pakistan, Nepal, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka, in forest, scrub, and even near farmland.
indian-pangolin.story: Domestic use and export of scales drive the decline. The species is more widespread than the Palawan endemic, which is why IUCN has not (yet) given it CR. That is not safety.
indian-pangolin.when: Endangered now. The Asian CR set is Chinese, Sunda, and Philippine; this is the remaining Asian species on the next rung.
indian-pangolin.humanRole: Trade in scales and meat, following the collapse of more easterly species.
indian-pangolin.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Manis crassicaudata, EN, 2019); IUCN SSC Pangolin Specialist Group; CITES Appendix I.

sumatran-tiger.hook: The last island tiger of Indonesia — a few hundred animals, listed Critically Endangered as a subspecies.
sumatran-tiger.imageAlt: A Sumatran tiger walking, showing a dense orange coat and many black stripes
sumatran-tiger.what: The Sumatran tiger is the only surviving island subspecies of Panthera tigris. IUCN assesses the tiger species as Endangered (2022) and has long treated P. t. sumatrae as Critically Endangered. Published island-wide figures disagree; conservation groups often work with a band of a few hundred (commonly cited around 400–600). There is no single agreed census. Javan and Balinese tigers are already extinct.
sumatran-tiger.range: Remaining forest blocks of Sumatra, especially landscape-scale parks such as Leuser, Kerinci Seblat, and Bukit Barisan Selatan. Gone from much of the lowland.
sumatran-tiger.story: Oil palm, pulp, roads, snares, and the trade in skins and bones isolated the last breeding groups. Prey is thin where forest is a patchwork. This is a different animal from the Amur tiger already on this shelf.
sumatran-tiger.when: Critically Endangered as a subspecies now.
sumatran-tiger.humanRole: Forest conversion and poaching on an island with no other tiger left.
sumatran-tiger.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Panthera tigris, EN, 2022; subspecies sumatrae CR in specialist assessments); WCS Indonesia landscape work.

rices-whale.hook: A baleen whale of the Gulf of Mexico, named in 2021 — NOAA’s best estimate is about 51.
rices-whale.imageAlt: A Rice’s whale at the surface in the Gulf of Mexico, photographed by NOAA
rices-whale.what: Rice’s whale is a recently described baleen whale (Balaenoptera ricei, 2021), split from Bryde’s whale. IUCN lists it as Critically Endangered. NOAA’s stock assessment still uses summer 2017 and 2018 oceanic surveys: best abundance 51 (CV 0.50), minimum 34. Newer survey data are being analysed; do not invent a higher total.
rices-whale.range: A narrow strip of the northeastern Gulf of Mexico, mainly off the Florida panhandle between roughly the 100- and 400-metre isobaths. Occasional records farther west do not make a second population.
rices-whale.story: Ship strikes, oil-and-gas noise and spills (including Deepwater Horizon), and a tiny gene pool are the documented pressures. The species was hiding in plain sight as “Gulf Bryde’s whales” until genetics and skulls separated it.
rices-whale.when: Critically Endangered now. On the order of fifty animals.
rices-whale.humanRole: Industrial use of a small, fixed feeding ground.
rices-whale.sourcesNote: NOAA Rice’s whale stock assessment (51, 2017–18 surveys); IUCN Red List (Balaenoptera ricei, CR); Rosel et al. 2021 description.

north-atlantic-right-whale.hook: A North Atlantic whale once hunted to the edge — NOAA’s 2024 estimate is 384, still Critically Endangered.
north-atlantic-right-whale.imageAlt: A North Atlantic right whale and calf at the surface
north-atlantic-right-whale.what: The North Atlantic right whale is a stocky baleen whale with callosities on the head. IUCN lists it as Critically Endangered. NOAA and the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium, using the Pace/Linden capture-recapture model, estimated 384 whales (+10/−9) alive at the start of 2024. About 70 are reproductively active females. That is a slight rise from the late-2010s crash, not a recovered ocean.
north-atlantic-right-whale.range: Calving off the southeastern United States; feeding in the Gulf of Maine, the Gulf of St Lawrence, and shifting northern grounds. Historically both sides of the North Atlantic; the eastern stock is effectively gone.
north-atlantic-right-whale.story: Basque and later Yankee whaling removed the easy coastal animals. Today the killers are fishing-gear entanglement and ship strikes. An Unusual Mortality Event has run since 2017. Eleven calves were logged in 2025, down from 20 in 2024.
north-atlantic-right-whale.when: Critically Endangered now. Low hundreds, few mothers.
north-atlantic-right-whale.humanRole: Historical whaling, then ropes and hulls on a whale that feeds and calves near shipping lanes.
north-atlantic-right-whale.sourcesNote: Linden 2025, NOAA TM NMFS-NE-338 (384 at start of 2024); NARWC 2025 report card; IUCN Red List (Eubalaena glacialis, CR).
